facts.title: Rise of the Album Format (Post-1965)
facts.body: Before 1965, musicians focused on gigs, with record sales as a secondary concern. The post-1965 era saw the ascendancy of the album and high-margin LPs over the 45 RPM single, making it possible for Rock and Roll musicians to achieve significant wealth from record sales. "Before it 1965, the goal of any musician was to keep working."

facts.title: Troubled Residency at Cafe Bizarre (December 1965)
facts.body: In December 1965, this "new and very weird group" secured their first regular gig at Cafe Bizarre in Greenwich Village, New York City. They were commissioned to perform six sets nightly, six nights a week, for five dollars per set. However, their avant-garde music often had the unintended effect of chasing away patrons rather than attracting them, leading to the band being fired at least once for driving customers away. "the band's music ten to do chase away patrons instead of luring them in and the band was fired at least once for driving away customers."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Discovery and Patronage by Andy Warhol (December 1965)
facts.body: One night, just as The Velvet Underground faced a second firing from Cafe Bizarre, Andy Warhol and his entourage, including groupies and "weirdos," unexpectedly visited the club. Warhol was so profoundly impressed by their "avant-garde approach to rock" that he immediately signed them to be his official house band at his performance art headquarters, The Factory, located on East 47th Street. Warhol assumed the roles of their patron, producer, and promoter, a pivotal moment that launched the band's "long, strange road to becoming legends as the first alternative rock band in history." "Andy Warhol adopts the Velvet Underground, thereby giving the band the break they needed, to eventually be hailed as the founders of alternative rock"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Formation as the First Alternative Rock Band (Spring 1965)
facts.body: The Velvet Underground began to form in the spring of 1965, with rehearsals starting that summer. By December 1965, their lineup was complete, and they are widely considered to be the first ever alternative rock band. "A few months later, Lew and his bandmate, the Welsh-born John Kale, would be part of what is considered to be the first ever alternative rock band, The Velvet Underground."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: First Paying Gig (December 11, 1965)
facts.body: The Velvet Underground played their first paying gig on December 11, 1965, at a high school in New Jersey. They were paid $75 for the performance. "They played their first paying gig on December 11, 1965. It was a high school in New Jersey and they were paid $75."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Formation in New York (1965)
facts.body: The core classic lineup of the band came together in April 1965 on a subway platform in New York City after Lou Reed encountered Sterling Morrison on the D-Train near 7th Avenue, leading to the band's formation. "The group came together in April 1965 on a subway platform in New York. Lou was going somewhere when he bumped into Morrison on the D-Train around 7th Avenue."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: First Live Gig (1965)
facts.body: The band's inaugural live performance took place at a high school in New Jersey in November 1965. "And the first live velvet skig was at a high school in New Jersey that November."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

facts.title: Appearance in 1965
facts.body: The band first appeared in 1965 during a time when rock and roll was considered disposable, AM radio-oriented, and not "serious music." Their arrival signaled a shift towards deeper, more sophisticated, and existential music that demanded respect. "When they first appeared in 1965, rock and roll, which is what we call the singles oriented music about basically cars and girls and that sort of thing, was still largely considered to be disposable, effervescent."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Unconventionality for 1965
facts.body: The Velvet Underground was an anomaly for their time, with a name derived from a trashy novel about BDSM, origins from the gritty streets of New York, and lyrical themes about sex, drugs, and eccentric street characters. They were so far removed from the mainstream "cars and girls" music that they were signed to a jazz label because no one knew how to categorize them. "The velvet underground was not normal for 1965."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Falling Spice Demos (1965)
facts.body: Under the name Falling Spice, the band self-produced material, including a famous demo tape recorded in their apartment in 1965. This demo featured early versions of tracks like "All Tomorrow's Parties," "Heroin," and "Venus in Furs," and represented a more intimate, poetic, and slower original vision for the band, resembling their later second album more than their debut with Nico. "con el nombre de Falling Spice ya tenemos material auto producido por ellos, tenemos esa famosa cinta pirata o esa famosa maqueta que se grabó en 1965 en su propia apartamento."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Velvet Underground: Una vision más humana que musical
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Demo Tape Journey to UK (1965)
facts.body: In 1965, John Cale took the Falling Spice demo tape to the United Kingdom, aiming to give it to Marianne Faithfull, Mick Jagger's partner, hoping she would pass it to Jagger or Andre Ollman (Andrew Loog Oldham) of The Rolling Stones. While the trip is confirmed, there is no evidence the tape ever left Faithfull's hands or reached Jagger. "John Kaley se la llevaría al reino unido en 1965 en uno de sus viajes para intentar darse la Marian Faithful."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Velvet Underground: Una vision más humana que musical
facts.name: The Velvet Underground

facts.title: Warhol's Patronage and The Factory Residency (Late 1965/Early 1966)
facts.body: Andy Warhol, impressed by The Velvet Underground's performance (likely in New York), immediately took the band, particularly John Cale and Lou Reed, under his wing, bringing them into his creative hub, The Factory. This marked the beginning of a profoundly difficult relationship between all parties. "Automáticamente coge la banda principalmente a John Kale y a Lou Reed y se los lleva a la factory."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Restored 1965 Ford Falcon Van
facts.body: Despite his rock star status, Dave Grohl's all-time favorite vehicle is a 1965 Ford Falcon van. He discovered the van in the Arizona desert with three flat tires, purchased it, and had it customized by King T's Customs in California. The original 85 horsepower inline 6 engine was replaced with a new V8, and the entire vehicle was restored and customized. "He likes his gunmetal grey 2002 BMW M5, but his all-time favorite is a 1965 Ford Falcon van."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: In late 1964, his mother Anne married Christopher Beverly, which explained why his mother was known as Anne Beverly while Sid's birth name remained Richie. Christopher Beverly died of cancer about six months after the wedding, a few weeks before paperwork could be filed for him to adopt Sid. "Christopher Richie died of cancer about six months after the wedding and a few weeks before the paperwork would be filed so he could adopt Sid."

facts.title: Shift Towards Album as Artistic Statement (Circa 1965)
facts.body: Around 1965, prominent artists such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Beach Boys began to pivot from focusing on individual singles towards conceptualizing albums as complete artistic statements, typically comprising ten, twelve, or more interconnected tracks. "But starting in around 1965, a number of artists, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, and the Beach Boys among them, began to think less in terms of individual songs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Bob Dylan

facts.title: Embracing Electric Guitar (1965)
facts.body: Bob Dylan's decision to start using an electric guitar in 1965 marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of popular music, signaling a new phase where the electric guitar became even more central to musical expression. This shift had a profound impact on the direction of folk and rock music. "And when Bob Dylan started using an electric guitar in 1965, we entered a whole new phase of evolution."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3
facts.name: Bob Dylan

facts.title: Shifting Album Perception (c. 1965)
facts.body: Around 1965, Bob Dylan, along with The Beatles, recognized the album's potential as a cohesive artistic work, which prompted a shift towards writing longer, more complex songs and sequenced collections rather than simply releasing singles. "The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and a few others looked at the album and thought, I can work with this."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Cautious Approach with Charlie Pride (1965)
facts.body: RCA, under legendary producer Chet Atkins, offered Charlie Pride a recording contract in 1965. However, the label adopted a very cautious approach initially, not using Pride's photo on promotional materials and testing audience reactions in different towns before scheduling further shows, due to concerns about his race. "Still, RCA, they took a very cautious approach with Pride at first."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Cassette Standardization (1965)

facts.title: Debut Album
facts.body: Released in 1965, this debut album was starkly different from mainstream rock and roll which focused on cars and girls; instead, it explored the gritty realities of New York City, including crime, weird sex, strange people, and drugs, which was considered too extreme at the time. Despite selling only about 30,000 copies between 1965 and 1970 and peaking at number 199 on the Billboard Top 200 album charts, its influence was immense, with producer Brian Eno famously stating that everyone who bought a copy started a band. "When their debut album arrived in 1965, rock and roll was largely about cars and girls and various escapists and fun topics. Not the velvet underground. They were from the gritty streets of New York City where there was crime, weird sex, strange people and drugs, lots and lots of drugs."

facts.body: The Rolling Stones' "Satisfaction" became a massive hit and solidified the distorted guitar sound's place at the forefront of rock music. facts.body: Dr. Robert Moog invented the Moog synthesizer in 1965, a crucial development because previous synthesizers were unwieldy, huge (the size of railway cars), heat-generating, and programmable only with hundreds of patch cords. Due to a subsequent legal dispute, Mick Jagger and Keith Richards ultimately gained 100% of the publishing rights and royalties from The Verve's song. "On this record was Andrew Luege Oldham's interpretation of the Stone Song the last time from 1965."

facts.body: This song by The Rolling Stones served as the original source for the melody sampled in The Verve's "Bitter Sweet Symphony." However, "The Last Time" itself was not entirely original; its core was based on a classic gospel song from the late 1950s called "Dismay Vide Last Time" (This May Be The Last Time). While the lyrics for "The Last Time" were largely derived from the gospel original, the melody was re-written by Keith Richards. Rights to this song (and other pre-1970 Rolling Stones material) were acquired by Allen Klein. "Esa rección evidentemente viene de un próximo original de los Rolling Stones en 1965 que es de Last Time y ahí hasta donde nos remontamos a la origen de la melodía de David점 Suits Symphony."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Title Theme
facts.body: Tom Jones, a singer from Wales, was recruited by John Barry to perform the title theme for the 1965 James Bond film "Thunderball." His powerful vocal performance contributed to the film's musical identity and continued the trend of grand, orchestrated themes for the franchise. "Barry went to Wales again for 1965's Thunderball getting Tom Jones to sing the title theme."

facts.title: Greatest Single
facts.body: Co-written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, this song was originally intended for The Righteous Brothers. The Animals heard Mann's piano demo and recorded their version first, shelving Mann's. The group significantly reworked the melody, lyrics, and completely excised an "overlong bridge," transforming a "decent song into a great one" and "one of the greatest singles of all time," despite Cynthia Weil's strong dislike of their changes. "We got to get out of this place, have been bitten by Barry Mann and Cynthia Wile, and had originally been intended for the righteous brothers, but they decided to have Mann record it himself."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Recorded in 1965 and featured on "The Fugs First Album," "CIA Man" is recognized as the first instance of anyone deliberately dropping an F-bomb on a rock and roll record. The use of such language was groundbreaking and controversial for its time, still necessitating censorship for broadcast decades later. "And that, as far as we know, is the first time anyone anywhere in the world dropped the F-bomb on a rock and roll record. Deliveredly."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts
facts.name: C.I.A. Man

facts.title: Malvina Reynolds Cover, UK Top 20
facts.body: This song, written by socialist activist Malvina Reynolds to oppose nuclear weapons testing, was learned by Chris Curtis from a Joan Baez album. It was The Searchers' first folk song released as a single and, despite its departure from their normal style and controversial subject matter, achieved a Top 20 position. "Even though it wasn't as big a success as some of their other hits, given how utterly different it was from their normal style and how controversial the subject was, getting it into the top 20 at all seems quite an achievement."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
